bridge: You can already distinguish HTTP request/response fields (N06), browser events (B01) and ownership policy (S06). The B01 local greeting page does not send an API request. Use this studio’s public page for a harmless page-load observation, or use the complete paper fixture below; interception setup is optional.
teaching:
A browser's Network panel records requests the browser makes. Open it before the action, then select a request and inspect method, target, headers, body and response. A screenshot of rendered content does not necessarily show what data crossed the boundary.

An intercepting proxy sits between a configured client and server and lets you inspect or modify authorised training traffic. HTTPS interception requires an explicit trust configuration in that training browser. Use a separate lab browser and follow the provider setup; installing a trust certificate in your everyday browser changes an important boundary.

Before changing a request, predict which server-side decision should change. Keep credentials and personal data out of saved evidence. Compare one field at a time so a changed result has an explainable cause. A proxy is an observation tool, not permission to test arbitrary hosts.

A proxy can hold a request before forwarding it: a page that spins may simply be waiting for that decision. Turning interception off usually forwards messages automatically; it does not necessarily stop HTTP-history logging. The built-in test browser is preconfigured for the proxy. Inspecting HTTPS through a trusted test proxy uses separate TLS connections; it does not decrypt an arbitrary connection without the relevant trust and routing setup. Use the current tutorial for version-specific labels. Use this studio’s public page to inspect a harmless GET request, or use the supplied paper fixture. Neither requires installing certificates or changing system trust. Incognito is a separate temporary browsing context, not anonymity or proof that every existing incognito cookie has been cleared. Changes in the Elements panel alter your local browser copy, not the server.
example:
Fictional baseline
GET /api/notes/1
Identity: A
Response: 200, note1 owned by A

One-variable training change
GET /api/notes/2
Identity: A unchanged
Expected: denial if note2 belongs to B
Record: request difference, response, policy explanation
explanation: The altered identifier tests ownership while keeping identity fixed. Changing both the session and target at once would obscure which change caused the response. A public page can legitimately return 200 without a session, so decide the expected policy before interpreting status codes.
exercise: Optional observed route: open this studio’s public page, open browser developer tools (often F12 or the browser’s More tools menu), select Network, then reload the page. Choose the public document request, not an account request. Record method, host, path, response status and Content-Type; omit cookies, authorisation headers and personal query values. If tools are unavailable, use the supplied paper fixture: GET https://notes.example/api/notes/1; response 200; Content-Type application/json; identity A; note1 owned by A. Label it hypothetical. Then change only the target to note2 owned by B and predict the decision.
solution: For the paper fixture: method GET, host notes.example, path /api/notes/1, status 200 and response type application/json. The same A identity requesting B’s note2 must be denied under the ownership rule. For an actual public document observation the values come from the selected request and may differ; public access can correctly return 200 without login. Mark observations and predictions separately. The B01 greeting click changes the DOM locally and supplies no HTTP API request to inspect.
challenge: Write a minimal evidence template for an authorised request test, including scope, baseline, one change, expected decision, actual decision and redaction. Explain why a redirect to an out-of-scope host is a stop-and-review event.
challenge_solution: A complete blank template is: authorised host/path and date; test account labels (no credentials); expected policy; baseline method/path and redacted inputs; one changed value; expected decision; observed status/body/state; reasoning; limitations. A redirect changes the target host, so check the scope before following it with testing tools. Permission for one application does not automatically cover another service.
